name: Treaty with the Quapaw, 1833
promises: Article I: the Quapaw gave up the land the Caddo had given them on Bayou Treache of the Red River, where floods had destroyed their crops and, the preamble says, nearly a quarter of the people had died.

Article II: the United States would convey by patent 150 sections of land west of the Missouri state line, between the Seneca and Shawnee lands, as a permanent home, and protect the Quapaw there from interruption or disturbance by any tribe or person.

Article III: removal at United States expense, a year of provisions, livestock, tools, guns and household goods, a farmer, a blacksmith, and $1,000 a year for education while the President judged it necessary.
Article IV: in place of their existing annuities, the United States would pay listed Quapaw debts up to $4,180, spend $1,000 on house building, and pay $2,000 a year for twenty years.

breaches.what: The Commission found that the United States agreed in Article II to convey 150 sections (96,000 acres) but conveyed only 82,808.23 acres in what is now northeastern Oklahoma and southeastern Kansas, a shortage of 13,191.77 acres, and that Congress paid $39,423.03 for the shortage by an act of 1891. It also held that the 1833 land could not be set off against the Quapaw award for the 1824 cession.

landTaken: The Article II home was delivered 13,191.77 acres short of the 96,000 acres promised (Commission findings, Docket 14).
compensation: Congress appropriated $39,423.03 for the 13,191.77 acres not conveyed, by the act of March 3, 1891, 26 Stat. 989, 998 (Commission findings, Docket 14). The Commission said the sum was accepted in lieu of the missing land.
today: In the same docket the Commission found that the Quapaw were paid an unconscionable consideration for the land they ceded in 1824 and refused to count the 1833 land as payment for it (Opinion of March 15, 1951 and Opinion of December 12, 1951).

openQuestions: treaties.json lists this entry under the schedule tribes "Kaskaskia; Mixed Seneka; Ottawa of Blanehard's fork..." but the date, Kappler page and text are the Quapaw treaty of May 13, 1833. The schedule tribes look copied from another entry.

The March 15, 1951 opinion gives the 1891 shortage payment as $39,575.31 in one sentence and $39,423.03 in another; the additional findings and the December 1951 opinion give $39,423.03, which is used here.
The collection dates the additional findings (item 349) 1995-12-06, which cannot be right for 1 Ind. Cl. Comm. 644; it was entered in the Docket 14 proceedings of 1951.
Whether the Article III goods, the education money and the twenty $2,000 annuities were delivered in full was not traced.
No history page from the Quapaw Nation about the 1833 treaty was found (quapawtribe.com history pages did not load their text).
